newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Big powers to appoint successor to Balkan envoy.
newsitem.headline: Big powers to appoint successor to Balkan envoy.

text.p: The major Western powers are preparing to name a new international envoy to Bosnia to take over the thankless task of lobbying for reconciliation among Bosnia's hostile factions, diplomats said on Thursday.

Carl Bildt, former Swedish prime minister, has had to postpone plans to step down as High Representative for months partly because Western countries have had trouble finding and agreeing on his successor.
"Some of the best candidates, the ones who have a knowledge of the region, know better than to accept this job," said one diplomat, who asked not to be named.
The Spanish ambassador to the United Nations, Carlos Westendorp, is touted as a top contender for the post, Western diplomats say.

Two other candidates said to be under consideration are former British defence secretary Michael Portillo -- he lost his seat in parliament in this month's election -- and former speaker of the Finnish parliament Ilka Souminen.
The Contact Group of the United States, Germany, France, Britain and Russia is expected to name the new High Representative at a meeting in Sintra, Portugal next week.

The German diplomat who serves as deputy High Representative, Michael Steiner, will also depart later this summer. Steiner was considered a candidate to replace Bildt at one point and Bosnian Moslem leaders backed his appointment.
Some diplomats in Sarajevo said choosing a little-known Spanish envoy without experience in the region could damage efforts to reunify the country at a time of deepening crisis.
"They are putting up someone who nobody has heard of, who knows nothing about the situation here. That is not the right message to be sending right now," said one Western diplomat.
Whoever succeeds Bildt will be inheriting a job that many say is impossible.

The new High Representative, who oversees the civilian aspects of the peace treaty, will be confronted with a troubled country dominated by nationalist parties and an international community preoccupied with other problems.
The mandate of the NATO-led peace force is due to expire in mid-1998 and the United States has yet to commit to an extension of the mission, casting a shadow over peace efforts.

Eighteen months after a peace treaty was signed, the inter-ethnic central cabinet and presidency are in a state of constant paralysis. Moslem, Croat and Serb representatives have failed to reach agreement on virtually every major issue.
Under the treaty, Bosnia is supposed to be a single state comprising autonomous Serb and Moslem-Croat territories.
But Bosnia has three currencies, three sets of car registration plates, two telephone networks and no functioning central bank.
More than half the workforce is unemployed and hundreds of thousands of embittered refugees have no prospect of returning to their pre-war homes.

Serb, Croat and Moslem nationalist parties rule what have become ethnic ghettoes, using their police and official media to crush opposition and prevent ethnic minorities from returning to their homes.
Bildt warned in his last report to the U.N. Security Council that Serb and Croat leaders were undermining the peace treaty through "creeping secessionism."
Bildt's critics have accused him of bowing to nationalist hardliners but his aides say the post lacks real power or leverage.
They say initiatives from the High Representative have often been blocked by the United States, which brokered the peace treaty and dominates the multinational peacekeeping force.
